D018-D013_h001.question: I’ve been struggling for about six months now—ever since a gas explosion at the municipal building where I work. I keep reliving it. Sometimes, when I hear a loud noise, I’m right back there—smelling the smoke, seeing flames. I freeze up like I’m trapped again. It only lasts a moment, but it’s terrifying. I didn’t used to be this way. I used to enjoy fixing cars on weekends, but now, I just don’t care. My wife notices. I even snap at her, blaming her for small things—like she could’ve stopped what happened. I know it’s not fair, but I feel like someone must’ve made a mistake that day. I’m always on edge, heart racing after the smallest scare, and it takes ages to calm down. But what’s worse is the numbness—the emptiness. I can’t shake the sadness. I cry sometimes for no reason. I’m tired all the time, sleep too much, and I can’t focus. I don’t want to see friends or go out. Honestly, I feel broken. I had the trauma, yes, but I don’t have all those PTSD symptoms clearly tied together—they don’t fully fit. Still, the low mood just sticks, longer than it should.
D018-D013_h001.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)

D018-D013_h002.question:
I’ve been having a really hard time since that night last semester—something happened, and I can’t stop feeling like it’s still happening. I’ll be in class or walking to the library, and suddenly I’m back there, heart racing, breathing fast, like I can’t tell what’s real. Loud noises, even a door slamming, make me jump—sometimes I flinch so hard I drop my phone. I keep replaying it, thinking I should’ve done something different. I blame myself, like I deserved it or could’ve stopped it. I’ve started skipping study groups and stopped answering my friends’ texts. It’s not that I don’t care about them—I just can’t handle being around people anymore. I’m always on edge, scared something bad’s going to happen again.  

But honestly, the worst part is how empty I feel. I can’t focus on lectures, can barely finish reading assignments. I lie in bed most days, even when I know I have exams. I don’t enjoy anything—not gaming, not even going out with my roommate. I feel hopeless, like nothing will ever get better. It’s been months, and while the trauma stuff is bad, my doctor said I don’t quite meet the full criteria for PTSD—most of my struggle now is the depression.
D018-D013_h002.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)

D018-D013_h003.question: I’ve been struggling ever since the car accident eight months ago. I keep reliving it—out of nowhere, I’m back in the moment, hearing the screech of brakes, feeling the impact. It knocks the breath out of me. I can’t listen to sirens or sudden horns; I flinch like I’m under attack. My wife says I’ve changed. I don’t laugh anymore. I don’t feel anything, not even when my son runs to me. It’s like joy is gone. I find myself blaming the other driver constantly—how careless he was, how it wouldn’t have happened if not for him. The fear from that moment hasn’t left me. But more than that, I can’t focus at work. Spreadsheets blur, emails take forever. My concentration is shot. I know I should be doing better, but I’m exhausted all the time, even if I sleep. I don’t want to get out of bed. I cry some mornings for no reason. The trauma is bad, but honestly, the heaviness—the sadness that won’t lift—that’s what’s breaking me. It’s not just the memories. It’s that nothing feels meaningful anymore.
D018-D013_h003.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)

D018-D013_h004.question:
I’ve been struggling for about six months now—ever since that trial where my client took his own life after I couldn’t get him the mental health resources he needed. I don’t sleep well. When someone walks into my office suddenly, I flinch hard—my heart races like I’m back in the courtroom that day. I keep forgetting where I put files, even basic things. It’s hard to focus, and I find myself blaming the system—judges, probation officers—anyone but me, I guess. I know it’s complicated, but sometimes I feel like if they’d just listened, he’d still be alive. I feel so… ashamed. Like I failed not just him, but myself.

But the worst part is how empty everything feels now. I used to care deeply about my cases. Now I sit at my desk and can’t bring myself to open a file. I don’t want to meet clients, don’t want to fight. My boss checked in last week, worried I’ve withdrawn. I can’t explain it—it’s not just the trauma. I’ve felt this heavy sadness for months, like I’m stuck, and nothing matters anymore. I’m not having flashbacks, and I don’t avoid reminders on purpose—it’s just… I don’t have the energy to feel anything at all.
D018-D013_h004.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)

D018-D013_h005.question:
I’ve been struggling a lot since the school lockdown incident last year—when the police came in, sirens blaring, students screaming. I wasn’t physically hurt, but I can’t stop reliving it. Certain sounds, like a fire alarm or a door slamming, make my chest tighten and my mind race. I’ve pulled away from friends—didn’t go to the PTA dinner, even skipped my sister’s birthday. It’s not that I don’t care; I just can’t stand being around people right now. I get angry—too angry—especially at the district officials. They minimized what happened, like it was just a drill. I feel this constant simmer, like I’m ready to snap.  

My thinking’s been foggy too. I’ll stare at emails for minutes, unable to process them. And if someone touches my shoulder unexpectedly, I jump like I’ve been shocked.  

But beyond all that, it’s the heaviness. I wake up feeling defeated, cry for no reason, can’t sleep or sleep too much. I’ve lost interest in everything—even things I used to love, like gardening with my husband. That part started *after* the lockdown, but honestly, I don’t feel haunted by the trauma every day the way I think I would if it were PTSD. It’s more that everything since then just feels… dark.
D018-D013_h005.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)

D018-D013_h006.question:
I’ve been feeling completely numb since the accident last year—sometimes I’ll be talking to my husband and suddenly I’m back in the car, smelling burnt rubber, my hands gripping the wheel like I’m about to crash all over again. It only lasts a few seconds, but I’ll snap out of it trembling. I can’t remember chunks of what happened that day, like the minutes right after impact—just pieces, but the rest is blank. I don’t feel close to anyone anymore, not even my husband. I want to love him, but it’s like something’s been switched off.

I avoid talking about the crash, and I get angry fast—last month I threw a glass when my sister touched my shoulder from behind. But honestly, the anger feels minor compared to how empty I’ve been. I cry every morning before work, can’t sleep, have no energy. I used to love my job, now I can’t get motivated to make calls. I don’t enjoy anything. The trauma’s there, but my doctor said I don’t quite meet the full criteria for PTSD—guess I’m just stuck in this dark fog, and nothing helps.
D018-D013_h006.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D013_h007.question:
I’ve been struggling for about six months now—ever since that storm chaser incident where we were caught in the tornado’s path. I still close my eyes and feel like I’m back there, heart pounding, wind screaming, my team yelling. Sometimes I’ll be at work, looking at radar data, and suddenly I’m not here—I’m in the truck again, soaked and shaking. I can’t talk about it. If someone asks, I shut down. Whole chunks of that day? I don’t remember. It’s like a black hole.  

I get jumpy—door slams, phones ringing, I flinch like I’ve been hit. Last week I threw a coffee mug when my son slammed his bedroom door. I didn’t mean to. I hate that I snapped, but I just… exploded.  

But more than that, I feel hollow. I got named Lead Forecaster last month—big promotion—but it didn’t matter. I stood there at the ceremony and felt nothing. My wife keeps saying, “You should be proud,” but I can’t summon it. I can’t feel joy, pride—nothing. I wake up tired, go to bed restless, and in between, everything feels heavy. The trauma’s part of it, sure, but this numbness, this exhaustion—it’s not just the flashbacks or the jumpiness. That’s not why I’m here—it’s because I can’t *live* anymore.
D018-D013_h007.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D013_h008.question:
I’ve been struggling for about six months now—ever since I had to fire one of our long-time line inspectors after catching a major defect that nearly slipped through. He broke down right there on the shop floor, yelling that his kids would go hungry. I keep replaying his face, his voice… but oddly, I can’t remember exactly what he said after that. It’s like my mind just blanks out that part.  

I avoid talking about it—don’t even like opening those reports on my computer. Loud noises at the plant make me flinch—last week a press machine slammed shut behind me and I practically jumped out of my boots. I’ve been snapping at my wife over little things, which isn’t like me.  

Mostly, though, I just feel… hollow. I don’t enjoy fixing cars in the garage anymore. I don’t feel much of anything. I wake up tired, go to bed heavy. I don’t cry, I don’t hope—just get through the day.  

It started after that incident, but I wouldn’t say I’m "haunted" by it exactly—more like I’m buried under sadness. The trauma stuff? Some of it’s there, but honestly, it’s the numbness and the weight dragging me down that feel dominant.
D018-D013_h008.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D013_h009.question:
I’ve been feeling numb for over a year now—ever since my studio caught fire and I barely got out. Sometimes I’m working on a piece, and suddenly I’m back there—the smoke, the heat, my hands won’t move like I need them to. It only lasts a few seconds, but it feels real. I avoid talking about it, even with friends. Honestly, I can’t remember much from right in the middle of it—just flashes.  

I’ve always taken pride in my designs, but even when a piece sells at a gallery, I don’t feel anything. No joy, no pride. It’s like I’m watching someone else’s life. I get irritated so easily now—my assistant asked me a simple question last week and I snapped at her. Then, later, a car backfired outside and I shook for twenty minutes, heart racing like I couldn’t breathe.  

I know something’s wrong. I thought maybe it was the trauma, but I don’t have nightmares every night or feel constantly on edge like some people describe. The sadness, the emptiness—that’s what’s constant. The trauma’s there, but it’s the weight of the depression that won’t let go.
D018-D013_h009.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D013_h010.question:
I’ve been feeling really down for about six months now, ever since… well, since the accident. I was driving back from a job site when a truck ran a red light and hit me head-on. I survived, but I keep replaying pieces of it—like the sound of metal crunching—but I can’t actually remember climbing out of the car. That gap bothers me, but other things just feel numb. 

I avoid driving, obviously, but even riding in a car makes my chest tighten and my hands shake. Loud noises scare me, and I stay really jumpy for ages afterward. I used to take pride in my garden designs—last spring I won a local award—but now, nothing feels rewarding. I don’t even go to sites I used to love.

I’ve lost my temper fast lately—a guy bumped me at the grocery store, and I nearly punched him. But honestly, the low mood is what’s worst. I don’t want to see friends, can’t sleep, and I feel worthless. It’s not that I’m haunted by memories—it’s more that I don’t care about anything anymore. I don’t think I’d qualify for PTSD, because it’s not the trauma itself overwhelming me now—it’s the depression that took over after.
D018-D013_h010.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D013_h011.question:
I’ve been struggling hard these past few months—really, the past year since… well, since the accident. I keep seeing flashes of it—cars skidding, the sound of glass—especially when I hear sirens or see ambulances. It wrecks me. I can’t even take the bus anymore or pass that intersection. I just can’t. I’ve stopped going to group study sessions because a few of the classmates were there that day, and talking about it just makes everything surge back.  

I keep thinking, what’s the point? The world feels like a minefield—like bad things just happen for no reason, and no one can protect you. I used to blame the driver, but honestly, I mostly blame the people who said it was safe to commute that way. They told us the roads were fine.  

I’ve been snapping at everyone—my mom, my tutor—just yelling for no reason. I hate it, but I feel so raw all the time.  

But more than that… I can’t study. I lie in bed all day, can’t focus, don’t care about passing the exam anymore. I cry for no reason. I haven’t showered in days. I know the accident messed me up, but I don’t have nightmares or flashbacks like people with PTSD do—I just feel… empty. Drained. Like I’ve lost everything, not just from the trauma, but from myself.
D018-D013_h011.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Major Depressive Disorder

D018-D013_h012.question:
I’ve been having these awful flashbacks—sometimes on the train, out of nowhere. I’ll suddenly feel like I’m back in that tunnel during the derailment, hearing the screeching, the passengers screaming. It only lasts a few seconds, but I lose focus, and that scares me. I don’t talk about it much, not even with my wife. I just shut down when it comes up.  

People keep asking if I’m okay, but they don’t get it. I used to trust my crew, my dispatcher—now I feel like everyone’s just waiting for me to fail. I even blamed the maintenance team for weeks, thinking they missed something. Still do, sometimes.  

And the anger… I blew up at a coworker last week over nothing. One minute we’re talking, the next I’m yelling. It’s not like me.  

But honestly, the worst part is how low I feel all the time. I don’t enjoy driving anymore. Can’t sleep, no appetite, just… empty. I thought this would pass, but it’s been six months. The flashbacks and avoidance are there, sure, but it’s not *just* the trauma—my whole life feels dark now. I went to counseling, and they said I don’t quite meet the full criteria for PTSD, but the depression… that’s real, and it’s crushing me.
D018-D013_h012.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Major Depressive Disorder

D018-D013_h013.question:
I’ve been struggling for about eight months now—ever since my wife passed suddenly in a car accident. I was driving. That’s something I can’t get past. I keep reliving it—sometimes out of nowhere, I feel like I’m back in the car, gripping the wheel, hearing the crash. It’s so real. I can’t be near that stretch of road now, or even get into the passenger seat. I avoid anything that reminds me of her, or that night.  

I don’t trust anyone anymore. I used to talk to my coworkers, but now I just push them away. Part of me believes I should’ve seen it coming—should’ve reacted faster. What kind of husband misses that?  

The anger scares me. I snapped at a guy from IT over a printer jam last week—threw a keyboard. I’ve never been like that. But honestly, the worst part is the emptiness. I can’t sleep, can’t focus on code—something I used to love. I don’t want to eat, don’t care about work, don’t even turn on the TV. It’s like everything’s gray. I know the accident messed me up, but I don’t think I’m having full-blown PTSD episodes—they said I’d need more symptoms for that. But the sadness… it’s constant. It started after the crash, yeah, but now it’s just… all there is.
D018-D013_h013.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Major Depressive Disorder

D018-D013_h014.question:
I’ve been struggling a lot since that night about six months ago—there are things I can’t stop remembering, like flashes of what happened. I get these sudden images that pop up when I’m just working at the café, and sometimes I break down while steaming milk. I try not to think about it, but it’s like my mind keeps going back, and I've started avoiding talking to people about how I feel. I don’t trust anyone anymore—I feel like everyone’s hiding something, like the world is just full of danger and nothing really matters. I’ve been angry too—last week I threw a plate when my roommate raised her voice, and I didn’t even mean to.  

But honestly, most days I’m just… numb. I don’t enjoy anything anymore—not music, not hanging out, not even coffee. I can’t get out of bed most mornings, and when I do, it’s like every task is impossible. I feel worthless, like I’m broken. I cry a lot, sleep too much, and I’ve lost weight because I don’t want to eat. It started after the trauma, but it’s not just about that one night—it’s everything now. I don’t have nightmares or feel “on edge” all the time, and I wouldn’t say the trauma fully took over my life the way it might in PTSD—I just feel deeply, persistently sad.
D018-D013_h014.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Major Depressive Disorder

D018-D013_h015.question:
I’ve been struggling for about six months now—ever since that night I got mugged on my way home from work. I still see his face sometimes when I pass that alley, even on a different street, and I get this wave of panic, like I can’t breathe. I try not to think about it, but it’s like my mind keeps going back there—so I’ve started avoiding certain subway stops, even if it means walking an extra 20 minutes. I used to journal before bed, but now I don’t even want to sit with my own thoughts.

I keep thinking: *I should’ve fought back. I should’ve seen it coming.* I know it sounds irrational, but I feel... ruined. Like I’m not the same person. I’ve always been in control, but now I snap at coworkers for tiny things—like someone mislabeled a task in the project tracker, and I shouted in a team meeting. I felt awful after, but I couldn’t stop myself.

But honestly, the anger’s not even the worst part. I don’t enjoy anything anymore. I call in sick even when I’m not. I lie in bed thinking I’m useless—to my job, to everyone. The trauma stuff’s there, but it’s not *just* that. It’s like the whole world’s gray, and I’ve felt this heavy sadness every single day. I don’t meet all those PTSD criteria—they don’t fit exactly. But this sadness? It never lets up.
D018-D013_h015.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Major Depressive Disorder

D018-D013_h016.question:
I’ve been a postman for 27 years—same route, same dogs, same mornings—used to be kind of comforting. But ever since that robbery at gunpoint last year, things just haven’t been right. I keep seeing it over and over—the mask, the shaking hands, the way my bag hit the pavement. It pops up out of nowhere, especially when I’m sorting mail. I started avoiding that neighborhood entirely, even swapped routes with a buddy. Can’t stand driving past it.  

At first, I blamed the store owner—he didn’t help, just locked his door. Then the cops, for not being there. Still do. And I’m always watching—checking exits, counting people in a room. My wife says I haven’t been myself. She’s right. I can’t sleep, don’t care about fishing, barely talk to the kids. I cry sometimes for no reason. Lost 15 pounds. Just feel… hollow.  

But honestly, it’s not the fear so much anymore—it’s the numbness, the guilt, the sadness. The flashbacks and checking? They’re there. But mostly, I just can’t get up in the morning. The trauma messed me up, sure—but what’s killing me now is this constant weight.
D018-D013_h016.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D013_h017.question:
I’ve been struggling for about the past six months, ever since that emergency landing—it didn’t end in serious injury, but I keep reliving it. I have these recurring dreams where the plane overruns the runway, people are screaming, and I wake up drenched in sweat, heart pounding. I avoid flying whenever possible now—call in sick, avoid crew calls, even avoid driving past the airport. It feels like a betrayal—*I* was in command. I should’ve handled it better. I replay every second, wondering if I could’ve done something differently.

At home, my wife says I’m distant, disconnected. I don’t enjoy anything anymore—not flying, not our weekend hikes, not even spending time with our grandson. I’m tired all the time, but I can’t sleep through the night. My appetite’s gone, and I’ve lost about fifteen pounds. I find myself scanning the room in restaurants, checking exits, noticing exits even mid-conversation—old habits, but now it’s constant. 

I know I’m not myself. I feel like a shell. But I also know that while the trauma weighs on me, these dreams and avoidance aren’t happening *only* about the event—and I don’t have flashbacks or constant hypervigilance. It’s more that everything feels meaningless now, like the joy’s been drained out of life.
D018-D013_h017.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D013_h018.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since that armed robbery at my restaurant six months ago. I still feel shaken—every time the door jingles loudly or someone stands too close to the register, my heart starts racing and I get this wave of panic. I didn’t used to be like this. I try not to think about it, but the memories sneak up—like when I pass by the spot where the robber stood. I just shut down, go quiet. I even catch myself avoiding the security monitor now, like if I don’t see it, it didn’t happen.  

I keep replaying it, and honestly, I blame my manager—he should’ve hit the silent alarm sooner. I know that’s not totally fair, but I can’t stop feeling that way. I check the exits every time I walk in, count the staff, make sure the phone’s within reach. But more than anything, I’m just… empty. I don’t enjoy cooking anymore, I barely have energy to get dressed, and I’ve lost so much weight. My husband says I’m not the same. I used to love running the place, but now I just drag myself through the day. The trauma changed everything, but what I feel most isn’t flashbacks or nightmares—it’s this deep, constant sadness, like I’m stuck underwater.
D018-D013_h018.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D013_h019.question:

D018-D013_h019.options:
